title: Two countries, one PPC each: opportunity cost, comparative advantage and terms of trade

stimulus.title: Corn and fabric in Kestria and Lomar

table.caption: The most corn or fabric one worker can produce in a day in two invented countries, Kestria and Lomar. Each country faces a constant opportunity cost.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Draw a correctly labeled production possibilities curve for Kestria, with corn on the horizontal axis and fabric on the vertical axis. Plot a point U that shows Kestria's output when some of its workers are unemployed.

rubric.point: A correctly labeled PPC: corn on the horizontal axis, fabric on the vertical axis, and the curve labeled PPC (or Kestria)
accept: a straight-line PPC from 36 bushels of corn to 12 bolts of fabric
axes labeled with the two goods by name

rubric.point: Point U plotted inside the PPC
accept: any point below and to the left of the curve

parts.sample: The horizontal axis is labeled Corn and the vertical axis Fabric. Kestria's PPC is a straight line from 12 bolts of fabric on the vertical axis to 36 bushels of corn on the horizontal axis (constant opportunity cost), labeled PPC. Point U sits inside the line, below and to the left of it, because unemployed workers mean Kestria produces less of both goods than it could.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate Lomar's opportunity cost of producing one bolt of fabric, in bushels of corn. Show your work.

rubric.point: 2 bushels of corn, with work shown (20 / 10)
accept: 20 bushels of corn given up for 10 bolts of fabric, so 2 bushels per bolt

parts.sample: A Lomar worker who makes 10 bolts of fabric gives up 20 bushels of corn, so one bolt costs $\frac{20}{10} = 2$ bushels of corn.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Identify the country that has the comparative advantage in producing corn. Explain using opportunity costs.

rubric.point: Kestria, because its opportunity cost of a bushel of corn (1/3 bolt of fabric) is lower than Lomar's (1/2 bolt)
accept: Kestria gives up less fabric per bushel of corn than Lomar
Kestria, with both opportunity costs correctly stated and compared

parts.sample: Kestria. One bushel of corn costs Kestria $\frac{12}{36}$, a third of a bolt of fabric, and costs Lomar $\frac{10}{20}$, half a bolt. Kestria's opportunity cost of corn is lower, so it has the comparative advantage in corn, even though it also has the absolute advantage in fabric.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Suppose Kestria and Lomar specialize and trade at 1 bolt of fabric for 2.5 bushels of corn. Will both countries gain from this trade? Explain.

rubric.point: Yes, with both sides explained: Lomar receives 2.5 bushels for a bolt that costs it 2 to make, and Kestria pays 2.5 bushels for a bolt that would cost it 3 to make
accept: Yes, because 2.5 bushels per bolt lies between the two opportunity costs of fabric (2 for Lomar and 3 for Kestria)

parts.sample: Yes. Lomar specializes in fabric, where a bolt costs it 2 bushels of corn; selling a bolt for 2.5 bushels gives it half a bushel more than it gave up. Kestria specializes in corn; making a bolt itself would cost 3 bushels, so buying one for 2.5 saves half a bushel. The terms lie between the two opportunity costs, so both gain.
